facts.statement: Neophrontops is an extinct genus classified within the Old World vulture subfamily Gypaetinae.
facts.quote: Neophrontops is an extinct genus of Old World vulture in the subfamily Gypaetinae.

facts.statement: Despite being classified with Old World vultures, Neophrontops was native to North America.
facts.quote: Although its classification places it among the Old World vultures, the genus was native to North America.

facts.statement: Six species of Neophrontops have been named, spanning from the Early Miocene to the Late Pleistocene.
facts.quote: Six species have been named, ranging in age from the Early Miocene to the Late Pleistocene.

facts.statement: All Neophrontops species except N. americanus are known only from fragmentary fossil remains.
facts.quote: All species of Neophrontops, with the exception of N. americanus are known solely from fragmentary fossil remains.

facts.statement: N. americanus is represented by well-preserved fossils from the late Middle to Late Pleistocene deposits of the La Brea Tar Pits in Southern California.
facts.quote: The latter is represented by well preserved material from the late Middle to Late Pleistocene deposits of the La Brea Tar Pits in Southern California.

facts.statement: N. dakotensis is known only from a distal humerus dating to the Early-Middle Pliocene.
facts.quote: N. dakotensis (Early-Middle Pliocene) Only known from a distal humerus

facts.statement: N. vetustus is known solely from a distal humerus that is morphologically similar to N. dakotensis but approximately half its size.
facts.quote: N. vetustus (Middle Miocene) Known solely from a distal humerus, morphologically similar to that of N. dakotensis with approximately half the size

facts.statement: The parent group of Neophrontops is Aegypiinae.
Neophrontops belongs to the family Accipitridae.
The type species of the genus Neophrontops is N. americanus.
Neophrontops lived from the Burdigalian to the Late Pleistocene, between 18.5 and 0.0117 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Burdigalian to Late Pleistocene (18.5 to 0.0117 million years ago)

facts.statement: Researchers have questioned whether all remains belong to a single species, noting that such a classification would imply an extraordinarily vast existence for one biological species.
facts.quote: The assignment of all remains to this species has been questioned, as it was noted that "if it had corresponded to one biological species, it would have had an extraordinary vast existence."
